paras: The Fayette whippings were the night flogging of a Black man and two or three Black women by a citizens' committee at Fayette, the seat of Howard County, Missouri, in early February 1903. The women were ordered out of town, at least twenty-five Black residents left within a day, and two of the women were whipped again near Myers about ten days later. A wire report of a "race war" ran nationally, while Missouri papers disputed that description and largely approved.

On January 27 Harry O'Donnell, a white visitor from Indiana, was killed in what the St. Louis Republic called a "negro resort" in Fayette, and O. L. Turner was later indicted for the killing. Less than a week later a courthouse mass meeting chaired by the Methodist pastor Fielding Marvin heard calls for a whipping post, which the lawyer R. C. Clark said state law forbade. The meeting instead named committees to order the "disreputable element" to leave or be publicly whipped; the New York Sun cited "the lawlessness of the blacks and their insolent bearing toward white women."

According to the Republic's correspondent, a Black man named Bill Smith said publicly that "no white man could whip him" and that the town constable ought to be "plugged." That night three men seized Smith in a saloon, bound and gagged him, and whipped him with buggy whips and leather tugs at an elm tree near the graveyard. The committee then took women from their beds to the north side of the courthouse, strapped them to a post, whipped them and told them to leave.

Smith resisted, and the wire said he was so weak from loss of blood that he was put to bed instead of being driven out. Two of the women left at once and at least twenty-five Black residents departed the next day, while a white man who had associated with Black residents barricaded himself in his house. On Tuesday night, February 17, two of the expelled women were taken from the home of a Black man named Elkin near Myers, whipped again and ordered away by men said to be prominent farmers. The Chariton Courier said instead that the men at the house escaped and one woman was caught and whipped.

No arrest of any whipper was reported, and the Republic wrote that the committee's membership "has been conveniently forgotten by everybody here." Smith himself was jailed on an old warrant charging hog stealing. About 300 citizens were reported to have pledged to rid the town of "objectionable characters," and white papers claimed that "better class" Black residents endorsed the action.

The February 9 Fayette dispatch declared that "a race war has been started" and ran under headlines such as "NEGRO WOMEN PUBLICLY WHIPPED" in the New-York Tribune and "WHIPPING OF NEGROES PRECIPITATES RACE WAR" in the Birmingham Age-Herald. The New York Sun's St. Louis account, "DRIVING OUT THE NEGROES," said the whippers were disguised as white caps.

Missouri coverage took a different line: the Republic's staff correspondent called the night a "social disturbance" and credited "the spirit of purification," and a Sunday feature called it "a necessary action in order to subdue the negroes." The Monroe City Democrat endorsed the whipping post, and the Chariton Courier ended its Myers item with "The way of the transgressor is hard." The Scott County Kicker mocked the Fayette papers' denial of a race war under the heading "'Lovely' at Fayette," a passage reprinted in North Carolina.

The Baltimore Afro-American ran the St. Louis account on its front page as "FORCED TO LEAVE BY BEST CITIZENS." The Professional World of Columbia, Missouri, called the beating of women "a disgrace to any people or community" and "semi-barbarous lawlessness." In late March the Montgomery Advertiser quoted the New York Independent's criticism and answered it by asking, "What would you do?"

The wire dated the whippings Friday night, February 6, but the Republic's correspondent wrote of Saturday night. The wire and the Afro-American counted a man and two women, while the Republic's correspondent at Fayette and the Fayette papers counted a man and three women. The Sun and the Afro-American described white-cap disguises, but the Republic twice said none were used.

reader.title: Fayette whippings (1903)
bases: A committee formed at a citizens' mass meeting whipped Black residents it called disreputable and ordered them out of town, and papers called the whippers 'white caps', 'whitecaps' and 'whitecappers' (A3, A6, A12).

The Fayette wire, the New York Sun's St. Louis version, a St. Louis Republic staff correspondent at Fayette, Missouri weeklies and the Black press all report the whippings, differing only in detail (A2, A3, A6, A10, A17).

accounts.label: Fayette wire (Feb. 9)
accounts.gist: A Law and Order League committee whipped three people, a man and two women, on the courthouse steps Friday night for 'alleged misconduct'; a 'race war' had started and 25 families had been frightened away.

accounts.label: St. Louis version (former Senator Clark)
accounts.gist: Men disguised as white caps dragged a man and two women from their homes and whipped them; the man fought and needed a physician; the women were ordered to leave.

accounts.label: St. Louis Republic staff correspondent
accounts.gist: After a mass meeting, an undisguised committee whipped Bill Smith at an elm tree and then three women at the courthouse; Smith was later jailed on an old warrant; 'respectable' Black residents were not in danger.

accounts.label: Fayette papers (as reported elsewhere)
accounts.gist: There was no race war; whites tied four people, a man and three women, to a tree and horsewhipped them until bloody.

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch correction (via Chariton Courier)
accounts.gist: No race war; the 'better class of negroes' sided with the Law and Order League against the 'disorderly element'.
